claims.text: Transition-metal catalytic performance is governed by in situ transient changes in surface oxidation state.
Transient surface oxidation-state changes dynamically modulate adsorbate binding energies.
Changes in adsorbate binding energies alter catalytic activity.
Changes in adsorbate binding energies alter catalytic selectivity and durability.
As-synthesized mixed-metal surfaces exhibit a baseline distribution of oxidation states before reaction initiation.
Systematic variation of temperature, gas composition, and partial pressure can induce transient surface oxidation-state changes.
Near-ambient-pressure XPS and XAS can monitor transient surface oxidation-state changes under reaction conditions.
XPS binding-energy shifts and XAS near-edge changes evidence changes in local oxidation state and electronic structure at active sites.
Reaction-condition-induced oxidation-state changes alter adsorbate binding strengths.
The balance between strong adsorption for reactant activation and weak adsorption for product formation or desorption influences catalytic activity.
The adsorption–desorption balance controls catalytic selectivity and durability.
Catalysts showing larger transient shifts toward higher oxidation states will have greater activity than catalysts with stable or minimally changing oxidation states.
Catalysts showing larger transient shifts toward higher oxidation states will have improved durability.
Transient shifts toward higher oxidation states will affect selectivity in a predictable manner.
Pretreatment or modification can suppress transient oxidation-state changes while retaining the same bulk composition.
The proposed mechanism should apply to dynamic mixed-metal catalysts under operando conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to stable or passivated catalyst surfaces, including oxides with fixed stoichiometry.
The quantitative relationship between oxidation-state dynamics and catalytic performance may vary with catalyst composition and reaction type.
A comparison of composition-matched catalysts with and without suppression of oxidation-state dynamics can test the hypothesis under otherwise identical conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if suppressing oxidation-state changes produces no significant correlation or measurable difference in activity, selectivity, or durability.
